I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.
Pricing: what belongs in the comparison

Help Scout’s pricing page displays Standard at $25 per user per month, with higher packages at $45 and $75. Confirm the billing term and exact WhatsApp configuration before budgeting. Five users at the displayed Standard unit price would represent $125 in user subscriptions, before any separately applicable charges.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A founder wants warehouse staff to help answer a few order questions each week. Price the access those occasional contributors require and compare it with the benefit of consolidating all support channels in one platform.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations
WhatFlow’s inbox has no seat fees, so additional store colleagues do not multiply the software bill. The merchant also retains full feature access at the chosen message volume.

Service-suite features can be valuable, but the buying question should begin with the cases the store actually handles. A short order question, a delivery exception and a multi-day dispute may need different processes. WhatFlow is attractive for the Shopify WhatsApp layer because staff can participate without a seat charge and use the complete feature set. Keep any existing service system that still solves a separate, important job.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

We built WhatFlow so the first plan does not feel like an intentionally incomplete product. Every feature is available whether the store chooses Free or the highest paid plan. The subscription choice changes messaging allowances and rates, not access to the inbox, Shopify integrations or other features. A merchant can start with one workflow and add another without purchasing a new feature edition.

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.

It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Keep three lines in the budget: the application, applicable WhatsApp delivery fees, and any separate implementation or services. Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules. The current installation terms and rate pages should be checked before committing a campaign budget.

A realistic Shopify scenario

A brand wants personalized journeys across web, app, email and WhatsApp. Distinguish that strategic platform purchase from the practical need to keep Shopify order conversations available to staff today.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations
WhatFlow offers Shopify-focused WhatsApp with a no-seat-fee inbox and complete feature access from the free plan upward, making the operational channel accessible without a wider platform migration.

An inbox is only one part of a customer journey. Someone still needs to know which order the customer means and what should happen next. For a Shopify merchant, that context is often more useful than adding another independent contact database. WhatFlow brings Shopify events, message templates and the human response into a focused operating workflow. Its native-feeling extensions matter because store staff already spend their day managing the underlying orders.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. My recommendation starts with the store’s actual work: the order that needs a message, the customer who replies and the colleague who has to help. A useful comparison should explain why our approach fits that work, while being honest about what the alternative does well.

Do not use a free email allowance as though it were a free WhatsApp package, or assume an email subscription automatically includes the desired WhatsApp sends.
A realistic Shopify scenario

A shopper receives an email campaign and a WhatsApp checkout reminder before buying. Agree which system owns suppression, audience updates and attribution, so the same order does not become two separate revenue claims.
What Klaviyo advertises today

Klaviyo's WhatsApp page describes marketing and utility messages, customer-data-driven segments, cart reminders and order or shipping updates. It also presents service conversations and connections between marketing and customer support. Confirm availability, plan terms and market-specific restrictions for your account during evaluation.

Those features make Klaviyo relevant when the team already depends on its profiles and marketing workflows. They do not automatically establish that every Shopify operational requirement is covered in the way your fulfillment team expects.
Where WhatFlow fits

The WhatFlow demo app starts with Shopify events and mapped message templates. Order confirmation, fulfillment and abandoned checkout are explicit automation types. That offers a concrete evaluation path for a store whose primary goal is to make those customer updates run consistently.
A store does not have to replace its email platform to test that approach. The important work is defining which system owns which messages and how overlapping follow-ups will be avoided.
Why WhatFlow is a strong fit for store operations

WhatFlow offers a practical way to add WhatsApp operations without replacing the store’s existing email platform. The free-forever storefront button, no-seat-fee inbox and all-features plans help keep that addition affordable.

The useful integration test starts after the message arrives. Open the Shopify order, check its current state and ask a second colleague to continue the conversation. An app can advertise Shopify connectivity while still making routine work awkward. WhatFlow’s extensions, store-event templates and Flow support are intended to keep that work close to the store. The demo screenshot shows a working configuration surface rather than a sales mockup.
Feature access and the people who use the inbox

The team inbox has no seat fees. If the founder, a support colleague and someone in fulfillment all need to participate, adding those people does not create a per-user WhatFlow subscription. That is particularly useful when store staff share responsibilities rather than operating a large formal support department.

The storefront WhatsApp buttons remain free forever and can fit the Shopify theme and design. The button is an entry point, not a promise of unlimited free automated sends. Automated messaging still follows the selected allowance and applicable delivery rules. Keeping those two costs separate makes the free offering easier to understand.

For a concrete baseline, consider 10,000 sent messages in a month. Among the listed WhatFlow plans, Growth produces an app-side cost of $29.00 at that volume. It is a planning example, not a combined quote for every possible message category or destination.

Meta pricing varies by destination and category, and some service or qualifying utility messages have different treatment. An app allowance does not override Meta’s rules.
